title: In the Land of Women
full_review:
"In the Land of Women" (Warner Bros.) is a well-intentioned, sometimes touching, reworking of the cherished formula of a jaundiced guy from the big city finding meaning from "ordinary people."

But unfortunately, its protagonist, Carter Webb (Adam Brody, late of TV's "The O.C."), is a writer of soft-porn films, an objectionable distraction from an otherwise likable story with honest emotions and characters with boundaries. Pacing, which could charitably be called gentle, also trips up the directorial debut of Jon Kasdan, who wrote the screenplay.

The film opens in Los Angeles with the sensitive Carter in tears as his actress-girlfriend, Sofia Bunuel (Elena Anaya), dumps him. Crushed by that circumstance as well as the pressures of his screenwriting job, he finds an escape when he learns that his grandmother, Phyllis (Olympia Dukakis), is gravely ill. When he arrives in a leafy suburb of Ann Arbor, Mich., to take care of her, he hopes to find time to write his long-delayed screenplay about "real life" at a progressive Los Angeles high school.

But he spends less time doing either task once he meets neighbor Sarah Hardwicke (Meg Ryan), whose outwardly neat and perfect life (and lawn landscaped to resemble a sort of Munchkinland) is just a superficial cover for deep conflicts with her 17-year-old daughter Lucy (Kristen Stewart), philandering husband (Clark Gregg, barely seen) and a diagnosis of breast cancer.

While Kasdan's original idea may have been to show Carter restoring his humanity by connecting to three generations of women, Carter concentrates most on Sarah with whom he has deep conversations. When she opens up about her husband's affair (not seen), she dissolves in tears and asks Carter for a chaste hug.

Since 26-year-old Carter never tells Sarah what he writes, she decides he's safe company for Lucy, so he takes the teenager and her precocious younger sister Paige (Makenzie Vega) to the mall. Later, Lucy invites him to a teen party that ends in a fistfight. But Lucy has inner turmoil as well, and when she tells Carter of her father's affair, she gives him a long kiss, which he admirably resists.

Everyone's libido is kept in check, Sarah's bout with cancer is treated frankly and without melodrama, and Phyllis reacts to the indignities of old age with sharp humor. All this adds up to a reasonably uplifting story, except for an explicit description of one of Carter's pornographic scenes. Were he a writer of schlocky romance novels or even an overwrought TV show for teens (such as, say, "The O.C." was), Kasdan could have made his point much more elegantly.

The film contains crude language, an instance of the f-word, a couple of crass expressions, some chemotherapy-related sickness, a brief violent scuffle, and pornography and adultery references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
